analysis.one_liner: Bars the SEC from ever requiring companies to report their supply-chain greenhouse gas emissions.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in May 2023 and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law that no company issuing stock can be required to disclose the greenhouse gas emissions of its value chain — the pollution generated by its suppliers, shipping, and customers, known as "Scope 3" emissions. For most large companies, those supply-chain emissions are far bigger than what the company itself emits directly. The bill was introduced by Rep. Ronny Jackson and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it sat with no further action until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Large emitters and their trade associations — oil and gas producers, utilities, manufacturers, and agribusiness — gain the most. They would be permanently shielded from any legal requirement to report the emissions generated across their supply chains, the largest share of most companies' carbon footprint. It also protects big retailers and food companies whose suppliers' emissions dominate their totals.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, and other large emitters

how_it_helps.text: It writes a permanent statutory ban on any securities-law requirement that a public company disclose the greenhouse gas emissions or energy use of its value chain (Scope 3 emissions), so no future SEC rule could impose one.

Because supply-chain emissions are typically the largest share of a large company's carbon footprint, the bill removes the part of climate disclosure that is most expensive and most revealing for major emitters.

analysis.who_pays: Investors and the public pay. Shareholders, lenders, and insurers would lose standardized, comparable data on the full climate exposure of the companies they own or underwrite, making it harder to price climate risk. Regulators and the public would also lose the information trail that disclosure rules are designed to create.

drawbacks.text: Companies and their suppliers argue Scope 3 measurement is costly and imprecise: supply-chain emissions are largely estimates, and forcing reporting could push compliance burdens onto thousands of small suppliers who did not sell stock to the public.
The ban is written as a permanent statutory prohibition rather than a rulemaking judgment, so even if measurement methods improve or investors demand the data, no regulator could require it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a genuine cost to companies in measuring supply-chain emissions, and much Scope 3 data is estimated rather than measured. But the bill does not balance that cost against any disclosure standard — it forecloses one entirely by statute. The clearest beneficiaries are the large emitters whose value-chain emissions would stay out of public view.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2023 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Ronny Jackson (R-TX) introduced the Scope 3 Act on May 2, 2023, joined by 24 cosponsors — 23 Republicans and 1 Democrat.
The bill's only action after introduction was referral to the House Committee on Financial Services on the same day.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed; the bill received no further activity through the end of the 118th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, no statutory ban was enacted, which preserves the legal possibility that a regulator could someday require value-chain emissions disclosure. In practice, though, the outcome changed little: the SEC's final climate-disclosure rule adopted in 2024 already dropped mandatory Scope 3 reporting, and that rule was stayed amid industry lawsuits, so large emitters ended up without Scope 3 mandates either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large emitters, who avoided disclosure either way

for.name: Rep. Ronny Jackson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar any securities-law requirement to disclose value-chain (Scope 3) emissions.

against.name: Rep. Patrick McHenry
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup after its referral.

sides.party_line_note: 23 of the bill's 24 cosponsors were Republicans, with a single Democratic cosponsor.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and other large emitters
industries.note: The bill would permanently shield them from any requirement to report the emissions of their supply chains, which for energy and manufacturing companies are the largest share of their carbon footprint. Blocking the data keeps investors, insurers, and the public from seeing the full climate exposure of these companies.

Scope 3 rules would push farm-level emissions data requests down onto suppliers; the bill forecloses that. The cost is that the public loses visibility into the agriculture sector's climate footprint.

industries.industry: Institutional investors and asset managers that use emissions data
industries.note: Many large investors rely on supply-chain emissions data to price climate risk and meet their own reporting commitments; a statutory ban forecloses standardized public data, leaving them to buy estimates from private vendors.
